questions.question: A displaced threshold reduces the length of runway available for landings. What use is permitted on the portion of runway behind a displaced threshold?
questions.correct_answer: Takeoffs in either direction, or landings from the opposite direction
distractors: Takeoffs in the direction of the displaced threshold only
Taxiing only, since the surface is not structurally rated for landing or takeoff
Landings from either direction
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the portion of runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction or landings from the opposite direction. It is not limited to taxiing, and landings are only permitted from the opposite direction, not from the direction of the displacement.

reference.text: The portion of runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction, or landings from the opposite direction.

questions.question: When arriving from the upwind side of a nontowered airport traffic pattern, what is one recommended method of entry?
questions.correct_answer: Cross over midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, then when clear of the pattern, descend to pattern altitude and turn right to enter on a 45° to the downwind leg at midfield
distractors: Descend directly to pattern altitude and enter on a base leg
Cross over midfield at pattern altitude and immediately turn downwind
Enter on a 45° to the upwind leg at pattern altitude
questions.explanation: The chapter describes crossing over midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, then when approximately 2 miles clear of the pattern, descending to pattern altitude and turning right to enter at 45° to the downwind leg at midfield. Entering at pattern altitude directly or entering on the upwind leg is not the recommended procedure.

reference.text: One method of entry from the opposite side of the pattern is to announce your intentions and cross over midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude…When well clear of the pattern—approximately 2 miles—scan carefully for traffic, descend to pattern altitude, then turn right to enter at 45° to the downwind leg at midfield.

questions.question: When exiting a runway, how does a pilot interpret the runway holding position markings, and is ATC clearance required to cross them?
questions.correct_answer: The aircraft approaches the dashed lines first; the entire aircraft must cross both the dashed and solid lines to be clear of the runway, and no ATC clearance is needed
distractors: The aircraft approaches the solid lines first, and must stop until ATC provides clearance to cross
The aircraft approaches the dashed lines first, and must stop until ATC provides clearance to cross
The aircraft approaches the solid lines first, and no clearance is needed since the aircraft is exiting
questions.explanation: When exiting the runway, the aircraft approaches the dashed lines first. The entire aircraft must cross both the dashed and solid lines to be clear of the runway. No ATC clearance is needed to cross when exiting. When approaching the runway (the opposite direction), the solid lines are encountered first and ATC clearance is required.

reference.text: When exiting the runway, the same markings will be seen except the aircraft will be approaching the double dashed lines. In order to be clear of the runway, the entire aircraft must cross both the dashed and solid lines. An ATC clearance is not needed to cross this marking when exiting the runway.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about LAHSO restrictions is correct?
questions.correct_answer: LAHSO are not authorized for student pilots who are performing a solo flight
distractors: LAHSO are authorized at night for properly rated non-student pilots
LAHSO are authorized on wet runways if the pilot has received ATC approval
Student pilots may participate in LAHSO only when a CFI is on board
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly states that LAHSO are not authorized for student pilots on solo flights, are generally not authorized at night, and are not authorized on wet runways. The text does not provide an exception for student pilots with a CFI on board.

reference.text: LAHSO are not authorized for student pilots who are performing a solo flight…Generally, LAHSO are not authorized at night…LAHSO are not authorized on wet runways.

questions.question: A VASI installation provides obstruction clearance within what spatial limits?
questions.correct_answer: Within 10° of the extended runway centerline and up to 4 NM from the runway threshold
distractors: Within 10° of the extended runway centerline and up to 10 NM from the runway threshold
Within 15° of the extended runway centerline and up to 4 NM from the runway threshold
Within 5° of the extended runway centerline and up to 3 NM from the runway threshold
questions.explanation: The chapter specifies that the VASI provides obstruction clearance within 10° of the extended runway centerline and up to 4 nautical miles from the runway threshold. The other options combine incorrect distance or angular values.

reference.text: The VASI provides obstruction clearance within 10° of the extended runway centerline and up to four nautical miles (NM) from the runway threshold.

questions.question: A pilot at night observes an airport beacon flashing white and yellow. What type of airport does this indicate?
distractors: A civilian land airport
A heliport
A military airport
questions.explanation: The chapter lists beacon color combinations: flashing white and green indicates a civilian land airport, white and yellow indicates a water airport, white/yellow/green indicates a heliport, and two quick white flashes alternating with green identifies a military airport.

reference.text: Flashing white and yellow for a water airport

questions.question: When contacting the tower controller after listening to ATIS, what should the pilot do?
questions.correct_answer: State the ATIS code letter received so the controller can verify the pilot has the current information
distractors: Request the controller to read back the current weather conditions for confirmation
State only 'ATIS received' without specifying the code letter
Wait for the controller to ask if the pilot has the current ATIS before stating the code
questions.explanation: The chapter states that upon contacting the tower controller, the pilot should state the ATIS code received (e.g., 'information Bravo'). This allows the controller to verify the pilot has the current weather and airport information without relaying it individually. Simply saying 'ATIS received' without the code does not allow verification.

reference.text: Upon contacting the tower controller, state information Bravo was received. This allows the tower controller to verify the pilot has the current local weather and airport information without having to state it all to each pilot who calls.

questions.question: Which wind condition presents the worst case scenario for wake turbulence on final approach?
distractors: A direct headwind
A strong crosswind from the right
A light quartering headwind
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies a light quartering tailwind as the worst case scenario because the wake vortices could be present along a significant portion of the final approach and extended centerline, not just in the touchdown zone. A headwind would push vortices away, and a crosswind moves vortices laterally but does not concentrate them along the approach path as effectively.

reference.text: A light quartering tailwind presents the worst case scenario as the wake vortices could be all present along a significant portion of the final approach and extended centerline and not just in the touchdown zone as typically expected.

questions.section: Holding Position Signs and Markings for an Instrument Landing System (ILS) Critical Area
questions.question: What do the ILS critical area holding position markings look like on the pavement?
questions.correct_answer: A horizontal yellow ladder extending across the width of the taxiway
distractors: Four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, extending across the taxiway
A single dashed yellow line extending across the taxiway
White characters on a red background painted on the left side of the taxiway centerline
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the ILS critical area holding position markings as appearing on the pavement as a horizontal yellow ladder extending across the width of the taxiway. The four-line solid/dashed pattern is the runway holding position marking, the single dashed line is for taxiway/taxiway intersections, and white-on-red characters describe a surface painted holding position sign.

reference.text: The holding position markings for the ILS critical area appear on the pavement as a horizontal yellow ladder extending across the width of the taxiway.

questions.question: When ATC issues a 'hold short' instruction, what is the pilot required to read back?
questions.correct_answer: The entire clearance and 'hold short' instruction, including the runway identifier and aircraft call sign
distractors: Only the runway identifier, acknowledged with 'roger'
The entire clearance, but the call sign may be omitted if the frequency is busy
Only 'hold short' and the runway identifier
questions.explanation: ATC is required to obtain a read-back of all runway 'hold short' instructions. The pilot must read back the entire clearance and 'hold short' instruction, including the runway identifier and aircraft call sign. Partial read-backs or omitting the call sign do not satisfy this requirement.

reference.text: you must read back the entire clearance and 'hold short' instruction, to include runway identifier and your call sign.

questions.question: If a pilot determines the aircraft will exit the runway end and enter an EMAS bed during an overrun, what actions should the pilot take?
questions.correct_answer: Continue maximum deceleration efforts, maintain runway centerline, and do not attempt to taxi once stopped
distractors: Apply nosewheel steering to steer the aircraft out of the EMAS bed to one side
Reduce braking to allow the EMAS bed to absorb the aircraft's momentum more gently
Shut down engines and apply the parking brake before entering the EMAS bed
questions.explanation: The chapter provides specific guidance: continue deceleration following rejected takeoff or maximum braking procedures, maintain runway centerline to maximize the EMAS bed's stopping capability, maintain deceleration efforts since the bed is passive, and once stopped, do not attempt to taxi or move the aircraft. Steering out of the bed or reducing braking would reduce effectiveness.

reference.text: Continue deceleration - Regardless of aircraft speed upon exiting the runway, continue to follow Rejected/Aborted Takeoff procedures…Maintain runway centerline…Maintain deceleration efforts…Once stopped, do not attempt to taxi or otherwise move the aircraft.

questions.question: At an airport with no tower, FSS, or UNICOM, what frequency and procedure should a pilot use for self-announcing?
distractors: Self-announce on UNICOM frequency 122.8
Use the tower frequency even though the tower is not in operation
Self-announce on the emergency frequency 121.5
questions.explanation: Figure 14-1 specifies that at an airport with no tower, FSS, or UNICOM, pilots should self-announce on MULTICOM frequency 122.9. UNICOM frequencies are used when a UNICOM station exists, the tower frequency is used when a tower exists but is not in operation, and 121.5 is for emergencies only.

reference.text: No tower, FSS, or UNICOM—Self-announce on MULTICOM frequency 122.9.

questions.question: On a segmented circle, what do the traffic pattern indicators indicate?
questions.correct_answer: The direction of turns when there is a variation from the normal left traffic pattern
distractors: The direction of the wind
The alignment of the landing strips
The recommended traffic pattern altitude
questions.explanation: The chapter states that traffic pattern indicators are arranged in pairs in conjunction with landing strip indicators and are used to indicate the direction of turns when there is a variation from the normal left traffic pattern. Wind direction is shown by wind direction indicators, landing strip alignment by landing strip indicators, and pattern altitude is not indicated by the segmented circle.

reference.text: Traffic pattern indicators are arranged in pairs in conjunction with landing strip indicators and used to indicate the direction of turns when there is a variation from the normal left traffic pattern.

questions.question: If both the transmitter and receiver are inoperative and a pilot needs to land at a towered airport, what should the pilot do?
questions.correct_answer: Remain outside of Class D airspace until the flow of traffic is determined, then enter the pattern and watch for light signals
distractors: Squawk 7700 and wait for a steady green light before entering Class D airspace
Enter Class D airspace immediately and orbit the tower until light signals are received
Remain outside Class D and land at the nearest nontowered airport since landing at a towered airport is not possible
questions.explanation: The chapter states that when both receiver and transmitter are inoperative, the pilot should remain outside Class D airspace until the flow of traffic is determined, then enter the pattern and watch for light signals. The text does not say landing at a towered airport is impossible; it provides a specific procedure. Squawking 7700 is for emergencies, and orbiting the tower without determining traffic flow first is not the recommended procedure.

reference.text: When both receiver and transmitter are inoperative, the pilot should remain outside of Class D airspace until the flow of traffic has been determined and then enter the pattern and watch for light signals.

questions.question: How are taxiway direction signs identified?
questions.correct_answer: Yellow background with black characters, with arrows indicating the direction of turn
distractors: Black background with yellow inscription and no arrows
Red background with white inscription
Yellow background with black characters and no arrows
questions.explanation: The chapter describes taxiway direction signs as having a yellow background with black characters, with arrows indicating the direction of turn. A black background with yellow inscription and no arrows describes a location sign. A red background with white inscription describes a mandatory instruction sign. Direction signs always include arrows.

reference.text: Taxiway direction signs have a yellow background and black characters, which identifies the designation or intersecting taxiways. Arrows indicate the direction of turn that would place the aircraft on the designated taxiway.

questions.question: What do runway distance remaining signs indicate?
questions.correct_answer: The distance of the remaining runway in thousands of feet
distractors: The distance of the remaining runway in hundreds of feet
The distance from the current position to the next taxiway intersection
The distance remaining to the nearest runway threshold
questions.explanation: The chapter states that runway distance remaining signs have a black background with a white number indicating the distance, in thousands of feet, of landing runway remaining. They do not indicate hundreds of feet, taxiway distances, or distance to a threshold.

reference.text: The number on the signs indicates the distance, in thousands of feet, of landing runway remaining.

questions.question: Why should a pilot also check the wind sock even when a tetrahedron is available at an airport?
questions.correct_answer: A tetrahedron can be manually set to align with the runway in use, so the wind sock provides actual wind information
distractors: The wind sock is more visible at night than the tetrahedron
The wind sock is calibrated to FAA standards while the tetrahedron is not
The tetrahedron only indicates wind direction and not velocity, while the wind sock indicates both
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that wind tees and tetrahedrons can swing freely and align with the wind, but they can also be manually set to align with the runway in use. For this reason, a pilot should also look at the wind sock for wind information if one is available. The other options give reasons not stated in the text.

reference.text: Since a wind tee or tetrahedron can also be manually set to align with the runway in use, a pilot should also look at the wind sock for wind information, if one is available.

questions.question: After receiving a 'line up and wait' instruction, if a takeoff clearance has not been received within a certain time, what should the pilot do?
questions.correct_answer: Contact ATC immediately if no takeoff clearance is received within 90 seconds
distractors: Contact ATC if no takeoff clearance is received within 60 seconds
Cancel the LUAW clearance and taxi clear of the runway after 2 minutes
Begin the takeoff roll if no clearance is received within 120 seconds
questions.explanation: The chapter specifies that if a takeoff clearance is not received within 90 seconds after receiving a 'line up and wait' instruction, the pilot should contact ATC immediately. The pilot should never begin takeoff without an explicit clearance, and taxiing off the runway without ATC instruction is not authorized.

reference.text: If a takeoff clearance is not received within 90 seconds after receiving the 'line up and wait' instruction, contact ATC immediately.
